That ruling reopened homepage band 8 on 21 August and required it to carry two stories 'both detailed further on the inner page'; the band shipped with its hook and its button, and the button has pointed at href="#" ever since. This file is the inner page. THE TWO STORIES ARE THE SPINE AND THE ORDER: the transformation first (barren ground into a Food Forest — the client's own proper noun, capitalised), then the place you can come to (overnight school camps and day visits for students AND EDUCATORS, team meetings and retreats). Neither is a section among several. RULINGS APPLIED: F-1 this page is the PLACE and /work/projects/farm-school stays the PROGRAMME; F-2 the page ends in a phone number, not a form; F-3 school camps ship with their hole named, not filled; F-4 the stay frames come from the owner's own Airbnb listings; F-5 the farm is at Ladpuri. D-07.3 governs the two readouts and is not re-litigated here. TWO FIGURES ARE NOT IN THIS FILE ON PURPOSE — the composted leaves and the honey are the Farm School page's figures, and the build resolves them out of data/work/projects/farm-school.json so that /farm structurally cannot disagree with the page they came from. That is the /impact architecture, applied to two figures instead of thirty-two, and it is here because F-1 splits one place across two pages and a split is exactly where numbers drift.

masthead.lead: Five acres of barren ground at Ladpuri, in the Mewat country where the Aravallis cross from Haryana into Rajasthan, ninety minutes from Delhi. One tree stood on it — which is the only reason the line above is not literally true, and the tree has earned the correction. It is now a Food Forest and a working farm, built with the people who live around it, and a place you can come to for a day, a night, or a season.

before.head:
A story of
change
before.lead: “So it's a story of transformation.” Those are the Executive Director's own words for this place and they are the right ones. Nothing here was improved. It was made — out of ground that had stopped being able to make anything, in a region that has had very little made in it.

context.h: Where this is happening, and why it counts double
context.p: Two things are true of this ground at once. It sits in the Aravallis — the oldest mountain range in India, running from the edge of Delhi down through Rajasthan into Gujarat, and presently being quarried for stone, mined and built on. And it sits in Mewat, which is among the poorest regions in the country: the district on the Haryana side of it has ranked at the very bottom of the national development tables. So this is not a demonstration plot in a comfortable place. It is five acres of a range under pressure, in a region with the least to spare, and it was built with the people who live around it rather than in spite of them.

frame.alt: Bare ground and low scrub at the edge of the farm, hills on the horizon

rows.p: That is what stood on five acres when this began — not a figure of speech, a count. Everything else in this page's inventory arrived after it, and the single tree is why the number that matters here is not five thousand but the distance between one and five thousand.

The labour, the knowledge of what this particular ground does in June, and the hands that put the mud houses up are local. Mewat is not a backdrop to this farm and the people here are not its beneficiaries; they are the reason there is anything to visit.

rows.h: Water first, before anything was planted
rows.p: Swales cut across the slope, bundhs to hold the runoff, ponds to keep it. On five acres in the Aravallis the limit is never sunlight and it is rarely soil — it is whether the rain that falls in three weeks is still there in March.

rows.h: Then trees, and then everything that follows trees
rows.p: Over five thousand of them, most native, because a native tree is the one the birds and the insects here already know what to do with. Shade came, then leaf litter, then soil, then the things that live in soil, then the birds — and the birds are now a reason people come.

rows.h: Permaculture, which here means the farm feeds itself
rows.p: Not a style of gardening. It is the rule that every output has to be some other part's input: leaves and dung into the vermicompost lab and out as soil, flowers into honey, rain into groundwater, fodder into milk and milk's waste back into the beds. A farm that buys its inputs has not closed the loop; it has moved it somewhere you cannot see.

rows.h: Mud houses, built out of the site itself
rows.p: Thatch over mud, with bottle glass set into the walls for light. They are not a rustic effect — they are the prototype being tested, and the test is that people sleep in them through an Aravalli summer and an Aravalli January.
A food forest is a succession, not a planting. The canopy going in now is for a farm nobody working here today will see at its best.

produce.h: What five barren acres now put on a table
produce.p: Two hundred amla, two hundred kinnow, two hundred moringa, and lemon — planted in counts rather than drifts, because an orchard you can count is one you can hold somebody responsible for. Beyond the orchard: vegetables and leafy greens from the beds, oranges, turmeric, microgreens under racks, honey from the hives and milk from the herd. Most of what the kitchen puts in front of a visiting group grew within sight of where they eat it, which is the shortest way to make the argument this farm exists to make.

frame.alt: Oranges ripening in dense clusters on the tree

counts.what: Lemon, and the rest of the orchard

forest.head:
What grows
there now
forest.lead: The inventory is the evidence. A barren field does not have a manifest, and everything in this one had to be put there and kept alive.

figures.label: Trees, most of them native
figures.period: as counted by the Executive Director, August 2026

figures.label: Saplings in the native nursery
figures.period: standing stock, no start year sourced

resolved.label: Dead leaves composted into soil on site

systems.p: Layered rather than planted in rows — canopy, understorey, ground. It is the part of the farm that is deliberately least like a field.
Grown to be eaten, including by the people staying here. What the kitchen serves is mostly what the beds produced that week.
Twenty cows. The milk, the butter and the ghee on the table are theirs, and the dung is where the compost cycle starts.
Small, and kept as part of the cycle rather than as a unit of production.
Twenty thousand saplings. It is what makes the tree count go up, and it is why plantings elsewhere can be native without a supply problem.
The farm's own waste stream, closed on the farm. Leaves and dung in at one end, soil out at the other.
Hives that have to be worked, not watched. They teach more about what a monoculture costs than any lesson does, without anybody saying the word.
Planted for the insects rather than for the look of it, which is why it is at its best when it looks untidy.
Fodder, grown without soil, to carry the herd through the months when nothing green will grow outside.

systems.h: Mud houses, and other permaculture prototypes
systems.p: Built to be lived in and then watched. A prototype that nobody sleeps in has not been tested.

works.head:
How the place
keeps itself
works.lead: None of this is a demonstration model. If a system stops producing, it stops teaching, and it gets fixed rather than relabelled.

frame.alt: Four people working along freshly drawn furrows, sowing by hand

rows.h: Water is caught where it falls
rows.p: Swales, bundhs and ponds, so that rain slows down and goes into the ground instead of off it. The farm's own supply is groundwater, and the works are what put it back.

rows.h: Waste is a raw material or it is a failure
rows.p: Leaves and dung go into the vermicompost lab and come out as the soil the beds are planted in. Nothing is carted off the farm to become somebody else's problem.

rows.h: Solar, and an honest amount of it
rows.p: Enough to matter, not enough to pretend the grid is not there. When the power goes, an inverter carries it — and out here the power goes.

come.head:
Live, Learn,
Lead
come.lead: The farm's own three words for what it is for, and they are also the three lengths of stay. Learn is a day; Live is a night; Lead is what a group of educators, or a small organisation, comes here to do with the rest of it. Every one of them starts with an enquiry rather than a booking form.

doors.name: Day visits, half a day or a whole one
doors.p: A bus and a packed lunch. Half-day exposure visits are the commonest shape and the widest door; a full day gets you the afternoon as well, which is when most of the farming actually happens. Open to schools and colleges, to families and individuals, and to educators on their own account rather than only as somebody's teacher.
doors.who: Schools, colleges, families, individuals — and teachers and facilitators, who are named in the brief as an audience of their own.

frame.alt: A facilitator and children standing around a farm plot

doors.name: Overnight school camps
doors.p: A night changes what a day out can be. The animals get fed twice, the dark is genuinely dark, and the sky over the Aravallis is the argument for coming that nobody has to be talked into. Groups sleep in the mud houses and the morning belongs to whoever is up for it.
doors.who: School groups staying over, and the reason most of them come back.

frame.alt: The mud houses lit from inside after dark, their windows warm against the field

doors.name: Retreats for small organisations
doors.p: There is a table under thatch with the field on three sides of it. Small organisations and groups come out for a day or two of their own work — the farm does not distinguish much between a school group and a board, and neither do the chores.
doors.who: Small organisations, teams and groups wanting the city to stop being the reference point.

frame.alt: An open pavilion under thatch, drapes tied back around a round table and chairs

doors.name: Stays and internships
doors.p: Weeks rather than hours. An internship is meant to end with a person running part of this place unsupervised; if it ends in a certificate, it was a longer day visit. Shorter stays are simply that — you sleep in a mud house and lend a hand with whatever the day is doing.
doors.who: Interns and researchers from India and abroad, and anyone who wants to stay.

frame.alt: Inside an A-frame mud house — a bed under the bamboo apex, a small window at the far end

activities.lead: None of this is laid on. It is the day's work, and a group joins it — which is why the list changes with the season and why nobody gets the same visit twice.

items.p: Peacocks, parrots and kingfishers, the butterfly garden, and what a food forest looks like when you are standing inside one rather than looking at a diagram.

Five thousand trees where there was one has made this a birding site in its own right. Peacocks, parrots and kingfishers are the easy ones; the list is longer every year, and that lengthening list is the most honest measure of the restoration anybody has.

items.h: Farming, with your hands in it
items.p: Sowing along the furrows, weeding the vegetable beds, harvesting whatever is ready. It is the farm's actual work and a group of forty makes a real dent in it.
Unglamorous, enormously popular, and the fastest way for a child to work out how big five acres actually is.

items.h: Food, from the ground it grew in
items.p: Cooked on the farm from what the beds produced that week. For a lot of children it is the first time the distance between a field and a plate has been short enough to see.
Feeding them, petting them, and finding out what twenty animals actually need every day. The dung goes to the compost, which is where most of the questions start.

items.h: The hives, and what they are for
items.p: Bees teach more about what a monoculture costs than any lesson does, without anybody having to say the word.
Leaves and dung in at one end of the vermicompost lab, soil out at the other. It is the whole argument of the farm in one shed.
Ninety minutes from Delhi is far enough to get the sky back. It is the thing overnight groups remember, and it costs nothing but the walk out to the field.
Put last deliberately, because it is what people describe first when they get home. There is no traffic under it. For a lot of visitors it is the loudest quiet they have ever sat in.

triad.p: A night on the farm, in a mud house, with the crickets going and no traffic under them.
Farming, food, water and waste, taught by a place that has to actually produce.
Educators and small organisations, using five acres as the room they think in.

conditions.head:
It is not
a hotel
conditions.lead: This is the part most places leave out, so it goes near the top rather than in a footnote. Everything here is true of the farm on a good day.

frame.alt: A washroom built into a mud wall, a basin and dried grass in the alcove

rows.p: This is agricultural land. There is an inverter, so you will not be left in the dark, but you will notice.

rows.h: There is no wi-fi, and no television
rows.p: Mobile data works. That is the whole provision, and for a good number of people it is the reason to come.
Drawn here and filtered for drinking. It is not bottled and it does not taste like a city's.

rows.h: The nearest shop is a couple of kilometres away
rows.p: Bring what you cannot do without. There is a working kitchen if you would rather cook, and food from the farm if you would not.

rows.h: The food is what the farm grew
rows.p: Cooked with what is local and mostly what is ours, which means the menu is the season rather than a list.
Cows, bees, birds, buffalo, goats and chickens, none of them arranged for visitors. Dogs are welcome to come with you.

conditions.quote: It's not a hotel, it's natural, it's rustic. It's a real farm.
conditions.quote_attr: Vimlendu Jha, on the farm's own listing

waiting.head:
What we cannot
tell you yet
waiting.lead: Two things a reader has every right to ask, which this page cannot answer today. They are named here rather than papered over, and each one is a single fact away from being answerable.

claims.what: How many students can sleep over, in what, and with how many adults. Overnight school camps are real and they run, but no capacity, no sleeping arrangement and no supervision ratio is written down anywhere we can cite.
claims.unlocks: One line — beds, buildings, ratio — and the school camp door stops being a description and becomes something a teacher can plan a term around.

claims.what: How many people have been through this farm. Every other item on the work register counts its participants. This one counts its compost.
claims.unlocks: One participation figure with a period, and the farm can be read alongside the rest of the work instead of beside it.

sheet.head:
The nursery,
the hives,
the herd
sheet.lead: Three of the systems, photographed here. They are the ones that produce something a visitor can hold, taste or carry away, which is why they are the ones a day visit almost always ends at.

sheet.note: No frame here carries a date, because no date on this page is sourced. What each one shows is what it says it shows.

act.head: Come and see
act.lead: There is no booking form, and that is deliberate — every way of coming here is different enough that it starts with a conversation. Say which of the four doors you mean and roughly when.
act.email_note: For school camps, courses and retreats, which are arranged rather than booked.

onward.p: The programme that runs here — the five C's, the courses, and what a stay is actually for.
The farm is one of the things Swechha does. The register is the rest of them.
